closed_trades.thesis: HPE is the most valuation-protected way to own the AI-server/networking buildout in a tape where reaccelerating inflation (CPI 4.27%) and a rising 10-year (4.56%) are punishing rich multiples. It trades at just ~12.2x forward earnings and 1.67x sales - the cheapest in the server group - after a record fiscal Q2 and the completed Juniper acquisition, which adds a scaled networking franchise. Sell-side has responded with a +40.5% 30-day upward EPS revision, yet the stock is consolidating (1m +1.4%) and sits 23.8% below its 52-week high, so estimates are rising while price has not re-rated. The same SMCI collapse (-29%) that helps Dell consolidates enterprise AI-server demand toward HPE as customers de-risk suppliers. With the last print already behind it (38 days ago) and no earnings inside the 40-day window, this is a clean cheap-re-rating swing.

Dell is the best risk/reward in an extended AI-server complex: it pairs elite momentum (+143% 3m, +202% 6m) with the cheapest valuation in the group (forward P/E ~20.9, P/S 2.2) and a constructive entry, having pulled back only 2.2% from its 20-day high while sitting 4.1% off its 52-week high near a buy point. The 29% collapse in Super Micro is a direct tailwind, consolidating enterprise/AI-server share toward Dell as customers de-risk suppliers. Q1 fundamentals (revenue $23.4B, net income $965M) confirm profitable scale, and the current tape ('Dell Stock Nears Buy Point') shows institutional demand building. With no earnings until 9/3, a 45-day swing captures the momentum leg without event risk.

improvements.note: Weekly self-review: Last Friday's (7/31) stated change was to explicitly ask, whenever a watchlist name's would_buy_at condition was met or nearly met and still wasn't bought, whether the fat-pitch bar itself is set too high for this account's stated purpose. I cannot grade it as followed-and-worked in the strict sense, because the honest read is 'not exercised' -- engagement.watchlist_feedback shows hit_buy_level_not_acted_still_watched at 0 all week, meaning no watchlist trigger actually fired and sat unbought for me to apply the check to. The two biggest watchlist movers this week, TEAM (+51.9%) and SNOW (+26.4%), both moved without ever reaching their stated levels (TEAM's whole move was today's 8/7 earnings gap; SNOW stayed priced at 146x forward earnings) -- extension, not a missed trigger, so the specific mechanism the change targeted never came up. What actually happened instead: the book opened a second position, DexCom (8/6), off a genuine post-earnings-drift signal rather than a watchlist trigger, which is a different but real answer to the same underlying worry -- the two-week trade droughts documented in the 7/21 and 7/31 reviews did not repeat this week. Track record is unchanged: still 2 closed trades (DELL -13.52, HPE -4.53), both from mid-July, anecdote-phase calibration -- BKR and DXCM are both still open, so there's no new win/loss evidence yet on whether this week's picks were actually good. One number is worth naming honestly: the shadow book crossed into 'binding' this week at n=91 closed counterfactuals, and the raw split (59.3% regret_miss vs 39.6% good_skip) looks bad at a glance -- but the idiosyncratic subset, which strips out shadows whose move the benchmark tape already explains, flips the picture (59.5% good_skip vs 37.8% regret among n=37 idiosyncratic cases). Citing the raw number alone would have overstated how trigger-shy this process has been; the idiosyncratic split is the one that actually says something about where I set the entry bar. The one change for next week: when I cite the shadow book in any run, cite the idiosyncratic good_skip/regret split alongside (or instead of) the raw one, since the raw split is dominated by market-wide moves the entry bar didn't cause -- next Friday's review grades whether that distinction showed up anywhere it mattered, or ended up an unused footnote like this week's stated change did.
